RFP positioning · per model

Where each opportunity sits, relative to the others

A RadViz plot: every feature each model actually uses (33–43 of them, depending on the model) sits around the circle as an anchor, sized by its real share of that model's split count. Each RFP is pulled toward the anchors it scores high on, weighted by how important that anchor really is — a feature the model rarely splits on can't tug a point as hard as a top driver. All 1,899 real training RFPs are plotted per tab, positioned from their actual feature values and rescaled outward so the point cloud uses the full circle, not just the middle — nothing here is simulated; overlapping dots read as density. Use the checkboxes to isolate booked or lost, the target markers to compare where each class centers, and the contour line to see where each class's density actually concentrates. Hover any dot for that RFP's full feature shape as a small star plot; hover any anchor for its exact importance. Education Foundation · L-202502-65199 (Association, 147 attendees / 119 rooms) is ringed as a walkthrough example — it's the real deal that most closely matches the shape of a typical mid-size Association RFP, and it was lost.

Centroids & density

Target markers show the average plotted position of each class — where the middle of the booked cloud sits vs. the middle of the lost cloud. Hover a marker for the count.

The colored outline traces where each class's density actually peaks. Formal cluster analysis (Gaussian-mixture BIC + DBSCAN) on these real positions found no well-separated multiple clusters in any of the four models — each is one dense cloud, sometimes elongated, not several distinct blobs — so this shows that one cloud's real shape rather than claiming clusters that aren't there.

All anchors, by importance

Anchors with enough angular room get an always-on label; hover any anchor dot to see the rest — dimmed rows below are dot-only.

    Reading this / how it's built

    Why RadViz, not t-SNE / UMAP / MDS: those techniques optimize an abstract 2D layout to preserve neighbor distances — the axes that come out don't correspond to any named feature, so you can't point at a spot on the plot and say "this is the meeting-space pull." RadViz keeps every anchor tied to one named, labeled feature: a point's position is the importance-weighted average of the anchors it scores high on. That's the mechanism this view needs.

    What's real: everything in this version. Every anchor shown is a feature the trained model actually splits on — walked node-by-node through every tree (quoted_adr 400 trees / 33 anchors, conversion 307 trees / 33 anchors, pickup_ipw 234 trees / 43 anchors, fnb 298 trees / 43 anchors; a handful of each model's remaining features are one-hot/encoded columns not present as their own CSV field, so they're excluded rather than faked). Wedge width and label percentage are both the literal, full-model importance share — no longer just "share among a top-8 subset." Every one of the 1,899 training RFPs (1,455 booked, 444 lost) is plotted at its own feature values — percentile-normalized (1st–99th, clipped) against the full 1,899 rows — plus one larger ringed dot marking the walkthrough example at that same real position. No synthetic sampling anywhere.

    Pull is importance-weighted: a dot's position is the average of anchor directions weighted by value × that anchor's real importance share, not value alone — otherwise a feature the model almost never splits on (several are near 0%) could tug a point as hard as the top driver, which would misrepresent what the model actually does.

    Centroids are the plain average plotted position of every real booked (or lost) RFP in the current tab — not a re-projection of class-average feature values, so they sit exactly where the eye would find the middle of each cloud.

    Why dots were bunched near the center, and the fix: a weighted average over 30+ anchors that mostly agree in direction rarely reaches the theoretical edge of the circle — pulls partially cancel across that many dimensions, so the raw math put every real point within roughly the inner third of the radius (median real distance from center was 13–25% of the max, depending on the model). That's mathematically correct but wastes most of the circle visually. Positions are now uniformly rescaled outward from the center, per tab, so the single farthest real point reaches the edge — a linear stretch that preserves every point's angle and every pair's relative distance exactly; nothing about which RFP is closer or farther from which anchor changes, only the zoom level.

    Density contours: each visible class gets one outline traced from a real density surface (points binned to a grid, smoothed, contoured at ~22% of that class's peak) — it shows where the class's mass actually concentrates. This isn't a stand-in for formal clustering: a Gaussian-mixture BIC scan and DBSCAN run directly on these real projected positions found no well-separated multiple clusters in any of the four models. Each is one dense cloud (elongated in conversion, where one feature dominates importance), plus a handful of small (20–50 RFP) outlier pockets in a couple of models — not distinct sub-clusters worth drawing separate boundaries around.

    One caveat: revenue_intensity — a top-3 feature in three of the four models — is derived from the proposed quote itself, which doesn't exist before pricing. It's flagged as target leakage in the underlying diagnostics; its pull on this plot is real but shouldn't be read as available signal before a rate is set.
